## NGO Website Development in India: Building the "About Us" and Governance Page — Trustees, Team, Auditors, Policies and What Not to Publish

An NGO's About page should answer one question for a cautious donor, CSR officer or journalist: "Who is actually behind this, and are they accountable?" To do that, it needs the legal identity of the organisation, the names and short biographies of its trustees or board members, the senior team, the auditor and bankers if you are comfortable naming them, links to key policies, and a route to ask questions. It should not publish home addresses, personal phone numbers, ID numbers or anything else that puts individuals at risk. This guide is for NGO founders, secretaries and communications leads who are working with an NGO website development team in India and want an About section that earns trust instead of just describing the mission.

### Who this guide is for

Your NGO is registered as a trust, a society or a Section 8 company, and you may hold 12A, 80G, FCRA or CSR-1 status. Your current About page is a paragraph about the founder's vision and a stock photo. Meanwhile, donors and corporate partners increasingly check an organisation online before they give. You want a page that stands up to that scrutiny, without turning your website into a legal filing cabinet.

## Why the About Page Matters More Than It Used To

Before giving, a donor typically looks for evidence that the organisation exists, is legitimate and is managed responsibly. A CSR officer doing due diligence will want the legal documents; a first-time individual donor wants reassurance; a journalist or a funder's analyst looks for names. Fake fundraising appeals circulate in India, so a visible and verifiable identity is a real protection, both for the public and for your own reputation. We deal with the contact side of this in our guide to [contact and grievance pages that build donor trust](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-contact-grievance-page-trust-safeguarding-2026), and with financial disclosure in [transparency and impact reporting](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026). This article covers the part in between: the people and the structure.

## Start With Your Legal Identity

State plainly what kind of organisation you are. The right wording depends on your registration:

- **Public charitable trust:** registered under the relevant state law (for Maharashtra, the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950) or as a private trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. Give the registration number and the registering authority.
- **Society:** registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, or a state equivalent. Give the registration number and year.
- **Section 8 company:** registered under the Companies Act, 2013. Give the CIN.

Then list only the registrations and approvals you actually hold, each with its number and, where relevant, validity dates:

- **PAN** of the organisation (the organisation's PAN is public information often printed on receipts).
- **12A and 80G** registration details, with validity period. These registrations now carry fixed validity periods and must be renewed, so check the current dates with your chartered accountant before publishing. Our [12A and 80G renewal checklist](/blog/12a-80g-renewal-checklist-ngos) covers the cycle.
- **FCRA** registration number, only if you hold one and only with the status shown on the government portal.
- **CSR-1** registration number, if you are listed to receive CSR funds.
- **NGO Darpan** unique ID, if registered. Our guide on [NGO Darpan registration](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-ngo-darpan-2026) explains it.

Do not claim a registration you do not hold or have applied for but not received. "Application submitted" is honest; "FCRA registered" is not. A donor who checks the official portal and finds a mismatch will not trust anything else on your site.

A useful device is to place the legal identity in a compact "At a glance" box near the top of the page and again in the site footer, so that it is visible without hunting.

## Trustees, Board and Governance

### What to publish

For each trustee, director or governing-body member, publish:

- Full name
- Role (chairperson, secretary, treasurer, member)
- A short biography of two or three sentences covering relevant experience, written in plain language
- A professional photograph, with their permission
- Optionally, the year they joined

If your governing body is large, show the officers prominently and list the rest more briefly. If your NGO has an advisory board, label it as such so that readers do not mistake advisers for legally responsible trustees.

### Why names matter

Anonymous governance is the clearest warning sign on a charity website. Showing real people, with real experience, who have agreed to be named, signals that someone stands behind the organisation. It also gives a CSR reviewer or funder a way to check independence: for example, whether the board has members beyond the founder's family. You do not need to boast about this; you need to be transparent about it.

### Describe how governance works

Add a short paragraph on how decisions are made: how often the board meets, who approves the budget, how conflicts of interest are handled, how new trustees are appointed. A few honest sentences are better than a grand statement. If you have written policies for these, link them rather than paraphrasing at length. If you do not have them yet, say nothing rather than invent them. A genuine TODO for your own team is to draft a conflict-of-interest policy and a whistleblower policy before you announce them.

## The Team: Showing the People Who Do the Work

The board sets direction; the team delivers programmes. Donors like to see the staff and field coordinators, since they are the people their money supports. A simple team section with a name, role and photograph builds a human connection. Some points to think about:

- **Get consent in writing** before publishing any photograph or name of staff or volunteers, and agree what may be shown.
- **Do not publish staff mobile numbers or personal emails.** Use role-based addresses (for example, a general contact or finance address) that survive staff turnover.
- **Be honest about size.** A team of five that reaches a thousand beneficiaries through volunteers and partners should say so, rather than imply a large staff.
- **Distinguish staff, volunteers and consultants.** A reader should understand who is employed and who is not.

## Auditor, Accounts and Public Documents

You do not have to publish every document, but a handful build credibility:

- The name of your statutory auditor or chartered accountant firm (with their consent).
- Links to the latest audited financial statements and annual report, ideally in PDF, with the financial year clearly labelled.
- Your registration certificates, if you are comfortable making scans available. Redact anything that is not meant to be public, such as bank account numbers.
- Your 12A and 80G certificates, if you want donors to be able to verify them.
- Policies that donors and partners commonly ask about: privacy, child protection and safeguarding where relevant, grievance redressal, and anti-fraud.

A note on file hygiene: label every file with the year and a plain name ("Audited-financials-2024-25.pdf"), keep older years in an archive, and never leave documents with metadata or comments that reveal internal notes. Our [donation transparency checklist](/blog/ngo-donation-transparency-checklist) lists documents donors typically look for.

## What Not to Publish: Protecting People

An About page is not a place to publish everything. Several items put individuals at risk or create legal exposure.

| Do not publish | Why |
|---|---|
| Home addresses of trustees or staff | Safety and harassment risk |
| Personal mobile numbers or personal emails | Spam, fraud and safety risk |
| Aadhaar numbers, trustees' personal PAN numbers or bank details | Identity theft and misuse |
| Signatures on scanned documents | Can be copied |
| Photographs of children or beneficiaries without proper consent | Safeguarding and legal issues |
| Internal minutes, salaries or donor lists | Confidentiality |

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 applies to personal data, and an NGO publishing information about identifiable people must have a lawful basis, usually consent for named individuals. Keep the information to what is necessary for transparency, and give people a way to ask for correction or removal. Our guide to [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026) goes deeper. This is general information and not legal advice; confirm with your own adviser.

For beneficiaries specifically, see our article on [beneficiary stories and photos with consent](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-beneficiary-stories-photos-consent-2026).

## How to Structure the Section

One long page can be hard to read on a phone. A workable structure for most NGOs:

1. **About us** — a short mission and history page that tells the story in plain language.
2. **Governance** — legal identity, trustees, how decisions are made.
3. **Our team** — staff and key volunteers.
4. **Reports and policies** — audited statements, annual reports, certificates, policies.
5. **Contact and grievance** — how to ask questions or complain.

Link these from the main navigation under a single "About" menu, and from the donation page so that a hesitating donor can verify you in one tap. Our guide on [NGO website navigation for donors, volunteers and CSR partners](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-navigation-menu-donors-volunteers-csr-partners-2026) shows how to arrange the menu.

## Writing It So People Believe It

**Be specific.** "Founded in 2011 by a group of teachers in Pune to run evening classes for children of construction workers" is stronger than "committed to empowering communities". Use only facts you can verify and, where you give numbers, name the period they cover.

**Avoid superlatives.** "India's leading" and "largest" invite doubt unless you can cite a source.

**Show change over time.** A short timeline with key milestones is believable and easy to scan.

**Keep it current.** An About page that lists a trustee who resigned two years ago looks neglected, and a stale page undermines every claim around it. Assign someone to review it at least once a year and after every board change. Put a "last updated" date on the governance and documents pages.

**Mind the tone.** Write for an intelligent stranger, not for your own members. Avoid jargon such as "holistic ecosystem" and "stakeholder synergy".

## Technical Notes for Your Developer

- **Use real text and real images.** Names, roles and biographies should be in the page's HTML, not embedded in a graphic, so that users with screen readers and search engines can read them. Add descriptive alternative text to photographs.
- **Mark up the organisation.** Organisation structured data (name, URL, logo, contact points and, where you wish, "sameAs" links to official profiles) helps search engines understand who you are. Mark up only what is visible on the page. Google documents the supported properties.
- **Make documents accessible.** PDFs should be searchable text rather than scanned images where possible, with meaningful file names. See our [accessibility checklist for NGO websites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-accessibility-donor-trust-2026).
- **Let staff update it.** Trustee changes and new reports should not require a developer. A content management setup with simple roles lets a designated person update the team and documents sections; see our guide to [CMS roles for NGO staff](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-cms-roles-staff-updates-2026).
- **Keep it fast on mobile.** Many donors will read it on a phone. Compress photographs, and avoid heavy slideshows. Our [low-bandwidth donor guide](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026) has specifics.
- **Check the links.** Registration numbers, FCRA status and portal links should be tested. A broken link to a certificate looks worse than none.

## A Short Checklist Before You Publish

1. Legal form, registration number and registering authority are correct.
2. Every registration listed (12A, 80G, FCRA, CSR-1, Darpan ID) is held, current and verifiable on the official portal.
3. Each trustee has agreed in writing to be named, with a photo and biography.
4. No personal addresses, mobile numbers or ID numbers are published.
5. The latest audited accounts and annual report are linked, with the year labelled.
6. Key policies exist, are dated and are linked.
7. The page names a role-based contact for questions and complaints.
8. Someone owns the page and has put a review date in their calendar.
9. The page was checked on a mid-range phone on mobile data.
10. Your chartered accountant or adviser has read the registration and tax statements.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What should an NGO's About page include?

Your legal identity and registration numbers, a short mission and history, the names and biographies of trustees or board members, the senior team, links to audited accounts and key policies, and a way to contact you with questions. Publish only registrations you actually hold.

### Do NGOs have to publish trustee names on their website?

Not as a general rule on the website itself, though registration and tax filings involve trustee details with the authorities. Publishing names with consent is good practice for donor trust, but check your own legal obligations with an adviser.

### Is it safe to publish trustees' photos and biographies?

It is generally safe when each person has consented and you limit the information to professional details. Do not publish home addresses, personal phone numbers or ID numbers.

### Should we upload our registration certificates?

Many NGOs do, to help donors and CSR reviewers verify them. Redact private details such as bank account numbers and consider whether signatures should be visible. Make sure the documents are current.

### How often should the governance page be updated?

At least once a year, and immediately after any change of trustees, auditor, registration status or policy. Add a "last updated" date to the page.

## Where to Start

Gather four things: your registration certificates, your current trustee list with written consents, your latest audited accounts, and the policies you actually have. With those on one desk, an NGO website development team can build the section in a short time, and you can decide for each item whether it belongs on the page.
